stem: When counseling a transplant candidate about long-term skin-cancer risk, which epidemiologic pattern aligns with standard references?

options.text: Basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma account for 95% of skin cancers in solid-organ transplant recipients
Melanoma accounts for 95% of skin cancers in solid-organ transplant recipients
Skin cancer is rare and accounts for less than 5% of malignancies in transplant recipients
Only squamous cell carcinoma occurs in transplant recipients

explanation.rationale_correct: Basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma account for 95% of all skin cancers in solid-organ transplant recipients.

rationale_incorrect.B: Nonmelanoma basal and squamous cell carcinomas predominate rather than melanoma alone.
rationale_incorrect.C: Skin cancer is the most common malignancy in transplant recipients, not a rare minority.
rationale_incorrect.D: Both basal cell and squamous cell carcinomas occur; squamous cell is seen more frequently than basal cell in recipients.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → skin cancer → Basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Squamous cell and basal cell carcinoma: account for 95% of all skin cancers in solid organ transplant recipients

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → skin cancer → basal/squamous cell carcinoma (95% of SOT skin cancers); PDF p. 280 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. 95% BCC/SCC epidemiology angle distinct from squamous-over-time teaching (cctc-1102) and sun-exposed site recall (cctc-3101); anchor verified on Cupples p. 280.

stem: A coordinator compares skin-cancer patterns in transplant recipients with the general population. Which statement aligns with standard references?

options.text: Squamous cell carcinoma is seen more frequently than basal cell carcinoma in transplant recipients, whereas basal cell is more common in the general population
Basal cell carcinoma is always more common than squamous cell in both populations
Neither basal nor squamous cell carcinoma occurs in transplant recipients
Melanoma is the only skin cancer that increases after transplantation

explanation.rationale_correct: In solid-organ transplant recipients, squamous cell carcinoma is seen more frequently than basal cell carcinoma, whereas in the general population basal cell carcinomas are more common than squamous cell carcinomas.

rationale_incorrect.B: The relative frequency of basal versus squamous cell carcinoma differs between transplant recipients and the general population.
rationale_incorrect.C: Basal and squamous cell carcinomas account for most skin cancers in recipients.
rationale_incorrect.D: Nonmelanoma basal and squamous cell carcinomas are the predominant transplant skin cancers discussed.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → skin cancer → Basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) seen more frequently than basal cell carcinoma (BCC) … In the general population, the opposite is true

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → skin cancer → SCC more frequent than BCC in SOT vs opposite in general population; PDF p. 280 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. SCC-versus-BCC frequency comparison distinct from 95% epidemiology recall (cctc-2105); anchor verified on Cupples p. 280.

stem: During pretransplant evaluation, which bone-health screening study aligns with standard references for establishing a baseline before transplantation?

options.text: DEXA scan of the lumbar spine and hip
No bone screening because transplantation prevents osteoporosis
Bone screening deferred until ten years after transplant only

explanation.rationale_correct: Bone health preservation includes screening for decreased bone mineral density with DEXA scan of the lumbar spine and hip, with baseline assessment obtained pretransplantation.

rationale_incorrect.B: Recipients are at increased bone-loss risk and require baseline bone assessment.
rationale_incorrect.C: DEXA densitometry is the referenced screening method rather than routine biopsy.
rationale_incorrect.D: Baseline DEXA is obtained pretransplant rather than deferred exclusively for a decade.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → Preserve bone health → Screen for decreased bone mineral density
primary_anchor.quote_hint: DEXA scan of the lumbar spine and hip … Baseline (pretransplantation)

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → Preserve bone health → DEXA lumbar spine/hip baseline pretransplant; PDF p. 322 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Baseline DEXA protocol angle distinct from risk-group bone densitometry (cctc-2052, p. 31) and osteopenia teaching (cctc-1047); anchor verified on Cupples p. 322.

stem: A heart transplant candidate asks which organ recipients have the highest skin-cancer incidence. Which counseling point aligns with standard references?

options.text: Incidence is highest in heart and lung transplant recipients
Incidence is highest only in kidney transplant recipients
Skin cancer incidence is equal across all organ types with no variation
Skin cancer does not occur in heart transplant recipients

explanation.rationale_correct: Skin cancer incidence is highest in heart and lung transplant recipients, followed in decreasing order by kidney and liver transplant recipients.

rationale_incorrect.B: Kidney recipients have lower incidence than heart and lung recipients in the referenced ordering.
rationale_incorrect.C: Incidence varies by transplant type rather than being uniform.
rationale_incorrect.D: Heart transplant recipients have among the highest skin-cancer incidence.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → skin cancer → Risk factors
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Incidence is highest in heart and lung transplant recipients, followed in decreasing order by kidney and liver transplant recipients

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → skin cancer risk factors → highest incidence in heart/lung recipients; PDF p. 280 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Organ-specific skin-cancer incidence counseling distinct from SCC/BCC frequency (cctc-2106); anchor verified on Cupples p. 280.
